    CISA warns of new Ivanti bug being exploited as latest Patch Tuesday breaks records
    therecord.media · 14 Oct 2026 12:35 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGScisacredential-theftcve-2026-104935cve-2026-96951data-exfiltrationeuropeivantiivanti-connect-securemicrosofttenableunauthenticated-remote-code-executionunited-statesvolexitywindows-shell
    In plain words

    U.S. cybersecurity officials warned that criminals are actively using a newly discovered flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure, software organizations use to let people connect to their work networks from elsewhere. The flaw can let an outsider run commands without signing in, and the attackers have sought passwords, copied data, altered records, and looked around victims’ networks. U.S. federal civilian agencies must install the fix by Friday, while other Ivanti customers are also urged to act because these products are widely used by governments worldwide. Microsoft also released fixes for more than 1,400 software flaws, including one already being used to trick people into opening harmful files or links.

    Summary
    CISA warns that attackers are actively exploiting a critical Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day for unauthenticated remote command execution, credential theft, and data exfiltration, and federal agencies must patch by Friday. The alert coincides with Microsoft’s record October Patch Tuesday, which fixes more than 1,400 flaws including an exploited Windows Shell security bypass.

    CISA warned that CVE-2026-104935, an Ivanti Connect Secure flaw rated 8.6 out of 10, is being actively exploited and ordered U.S. federal civilian agencies to patch it by Friday. The flaw permits an unauthenticated remote party to execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti said it is working with a limited number of customers affected by exploitation, while cybersecurity firms also confirmed attacks in the wild.

    Volexity began investigating suspicious activity on October 5 that had affected a fully patched Ivanti VPN appliance beginning two days earlier. It identified three zero-day exploits; Ivanti patched two on Tuesday and was working on a fix for the third. The observed activity involved credential theft, data exfiltration, log tampering, and network reconnaissance, though responders found no malware that would allow continued actions without exploiting the appliance again. Volexity assessed with low confidence that the actor had criminal rather than espionage motives.

    CISA also added an actively exploited Windows Shell security-feature bypass, CVE-2026-96951, to its warnings, with federal agencies likewise required to patch by Friday. Microsoft said exploitation requires persuading a user to open attacker-controlled content, such as through a malicious link or attachment. The flaw was among 1,407 CVEs fixed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday release, a monthly total experts said surpassed the prior record of 973 and exceeded the 1,261 CVEs Microsoft fixed in all of 2020.

    • The Ivanti activity affected a fully patched appliance before the newly discovered flaws were fixed, showing that existing patch status alone did not protect against these zero-day issues.
    • Volexity did not find malware that would let the attackers continue acting without exploiting the Ivanti appliance again, which distinguishes the observed activity from an intrusion with identified persistent malware.
    • This is the sixth Ivanti flaw added to CISA’s exploited-vulnerability list in 2026, underscoring the repeated targeting of Ivanti products used by governments.
    • Microsoft’s October release fixed 1,407 CVEs, exceeding not only the prior monthly record of 973 but also the 1,261 CVEs Microsoft fixed across all of 2020.
    Key Points
    • 01CISA warned that CVE-2026-104935, an actively exploited Ivanti Connect Secure flaw rated 8.6 out of 10, allows unauthenticated remote execution of arbitrary commands and gave federal civilian agencies until Friday to patch it.
    • 02Volexity investigated activity affecting a fully patched Ivanti VPN appliance beginning October 3 and identified three zero-day exploits, two of which Ivanti patched on Tuesday while it works on a fix for the third.
    • 03The observed Ivanti intrusions focused on credential theft, data exfiltration, log tampering, and network reconnaissance, and Volexity assessed with low confidence that the actor’s motivations were criminal rather than espionage-related.
    • 04CISA also warned of active exploitation of CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass rated 8.8 out of 10 that can be triggered when a user is persuaded to open malicious content.
    • 05Microsoft's October Patch Tuesday addressed 1,407 CVEs, which experts said exceeded the previous monthly record of 973 and surpassed the 1,261 CVEs Microsoft patched during all of 2020.

    CISA Urges Immediate Ivanti Connect Secure Updates as Honeypots Log 105 Exploit Attempts

    In plain words

    A serious flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure, software organizations use to let people connect to company systems remotely, is already being used by attackers. The U.S. cyber agency CISA says affected organizations should update immediately because attackers can get in without a password, steal account details and data, and take control of the device. Security researchers have already recorded more than 100 attempts to use the flaw, raising the risk of wider break-ins if organizations do not fix it.

    Summary
    CISA urges immediate patching of actively exploited CVE-2026-104935 in Ivanti Connect Secure, an authentication bypass that enables unauthenticated remote command execution. Threat actors have already used it to steal credentials and exfiltrate data, with honeypots recording more than 100 exploit attempts.

    CISA urged organizations to immediately update Ivanti Connect Secure deployments after disclosure of CVE-2026-104935, an actively exploited authentication-bypass flaw. The vulnerability affects specified 25.1 and 22.8R2 releases and can allow a remote attacker without credentials to run arbitrary commands. CISA said attackers have used it for credential theft and data exfiltration, and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

    CISA advised organizations that find evidence of compromise to back up configurations, factory-reset or rebuild appliances, update them, restore configurations, and reset accounts, certificates, API keys, and license-server credentials. Previdian observed 105 exploitation attempts from 50 IP addresses as of October 14, 2026, including attempts using the X-DSCGI-PATH header to upload Perl scripts disguised as ZIP files. Volexity said UTA0576 chained the flaw with a privilege-escalation issue to gain root-level code execution and then performed credential extraction, reconnaissance, LDAP packet capture, and searches for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

    • Patching alone may not be sufficient after a compromise: CISA advises factory-resetting or rebuilding affected systems, restoring a backed-up configuration, and resetting passwords, certificates, API keys, and license-server credentials.
    • Organizations may need network and memory forensics to establish whether the flaw was exploited, indicating that ordinary appliance review may not be enough to find evidence of compromise.
    • Observed attempts used the X-DSCGI-PATH header to access an internal CGI handler and upload Perl scripts disguised as ZIP files, with returned markers used to confirm whether remote code execution worked.
    • Although some captured honeypot payloads were primarily testing for command execution, Volexity documented a separate actor performing credential extraction, Active Directory metadata theft, LDAP packet capture, and searches for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.
    • Ivanti Connect Secure version 22.8 is scheduled to reach end of life on January 31, 2027, so affected organizations using that branch need to consider the vendor's upgrade and migration guidance as part of remediation.
    Key Points
    • 01CISA urged organizations to immediately update Ivanti Connect Secure after the active exploitation of CVE-2026-104935, an authentication-bypass flaw that can enable unauthenticated remote command execution.
    • 02CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure versions 25.1.1.1 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 22.8R2.4 and earlier, and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
    • 03CISA said threat actors are using the flaw for credential theft and data exfiltration, and advised affected organizations to use network and memory forensics to determine whether they were compromised.
    • 04Previdian recorded 105 exploitation attempts against its honeypots from 50 unique IP addresses as of October 14, 2026, with the IP addresses geolocated to Singapore and the United States.
    • 05Volexity observed UTA0576 exploiting the flaw with a privilege-escalation vulnerability to obtain root-level code execution, then extracting appliance credentials and conducting reconnaissance and credential-focused activity.

In plain words

U.S. officials and Ivanti are urging organizations to quickly update Ivanti Connect Secure, a system used to provide remote access to company networks, because attackers have been using a newly found flaw since early October. The flaw can let someone outside an organization run commands on an affected system without logging in, potentially gaining full control and stealing sensitive information such as account passwords and device recovery keys. Federal agencies must fix it by Friday, and other organizations using the product are also being told to check for signs that they were already affected.

Summary
CISA and Ivanti urge immediate patching of CVE-2026-104935 in Ivanti Connect Secure, a zero-day authentication bypass actively exploited to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution and steal credentials. Organizations should update affected appliances, investigate for compromise with network and memory forensics, and rebuild/reset credentials if intrusion is found.

CISA urged organizations to immediately patch CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity authentication-bypass flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure that has been exploited in zero-day attacks since at least October 1. The flaw allows remote, unprivileged attackers to execute arbitrary commands without user interaction. Ivanti released fixed Connect Secure versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1, and 25.1.1.2 and warned customers to act immediately because exploitation in the wild is limited. CISA added the issue to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and directed federal civilian agencies to secure their systems by Friday.

Volexity reported that UTA0576 has chained the authentication bypass and remote-code-execution issues tracked under CVE-2026-104935 with a separate privilege-escalation flaw since at least October 3, reaching unauthenticated root-level code execution. The actor targeted Active Directory credentials and secrets, including LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, while CISA also warned of credential theft and data exfiltration. CISA said Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not reveal evidence because attacker commands execute in memory, making network and memory forensics necessary for compromise assessment. For compromised appliances, CISA advises backing up the configuration, factory-resetting or rebuilding and upgrading the system, restoring the backup, and resetting passwords, certificates, API keys, and license-server credentials.

  • A standard Ivanti Integrity Checker scan may miss this compromise because the attackers' commands execute in memory, so CISA says network and memory forensics are needed to look for evidence.
  • For confirmed compromise, CISA recommends more than applying the patch: organizations should back up the configuration, factory-reset or rebuild the appliance, restore the configuration, and rotate passwords, certificates, API keys, and license-server credentials.
  • The reported attack chain reached unauthenticated root-level control by combining the authentication bypass and remote code execution associated with CVE-2026-104935 with a separate privilege-escalation flaw.
  • Shadowserver observed more than 5,600 internet-exposed hosts with Ivanti Connect Secure fingerprints, although the article notes this does not establish how many are vulnerable, patched, or honeypots.
Key Points
  • 01CISA urged organizations to immediately patch CVE-2026-104935, an Ivanti Connect Secure authentication-bypass flaw that has been exploited as a zero-day since at least October 1.
  • 02Ivanti released Connect Secure versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1, and 25.1.1.2 to address the flaw and said exploitation in the wild was limited.
  • 03Volexity reported that a threat actor it tracks as UTA0576 chained CVE-2026-104935 with two other flaws to obtain unauthenticated root-level code execution and target Active Directory credentials, LAPS passwords, and BitLocker recovery keys.
  • 04CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and directed U.S. federal civilian agencies to secure affected systems by Friday.
  • 05CISA said organizations investigating possible compromise need network and memory forensics because Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool may not detect commands that attackers executed in memory.

    In plain words

    Cisco fixed a newly discovered flaw in its Secure Email Gateway systems that attackers are already using. A criminal can send a specially made email attachment to an unpatched system and then take full control of the computer running it. Organizations using affected Cisco email-security devices need to install the fix and check for signs of misuse, because an intruder with full control could remove evidence of what they did. Cisco says it has protected its cloud-hosted systems and contacted customers where it found possible signs of compromise.

    Summary
    Cisco patched CVE-2026-76519, an actively exploited Secure Email Gateway zero-day that lets unauthenticated attackers use a malicious email attachment to execute commands as root. Affected organizations should urgently upgrade Content Scanner Tools, check Cisco’s compromise indicators, and rotate credentials if compromise is suspected.

    Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76519, an actively exploited zero-day in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) products. The flaw affects the Advanced Malware Protection feature and can allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files and run commands with root-level control of the underlying operating system. Cisco said exploitation requires sending a maliciously crafted email attachment through an unpatched device.

    Affected SEG systems have the File Reputation service enabled and assigned to a mail policy while running Content Scanner Tools earlier than version 25.3.0.5525. Cisco advises administrators to check their scanner version and File Reputation settings, inspect the provided compromise indicators, upgrade to a fixed release, and review firewall and network logs for suspicious external transfers. Because attackers may remove evidence after obtaining root access, Cisco recommends that potentially compromised customers renew credentials and cryptographic materials, restrict appliance access, and use robust access controls.

    • Exposure depends on both configuration and software version: Secure Email Gateway instances are affected only when File Reputation is enabled and assigned to a mail policy while Content Scanner Tools is older than 25.3.0.5525.
    • Cisco warns that attackers may erase evidence after gaining full control, so a clean appliance scan does not remove the need to review firewall and network logs for suspicious transfers to external IP addresses.
    • For customers Cisco contacted about possible compromise, the recommended recovery goes beyond patching and includes renewing credentials and cryptographic materials and restricting access to the appliance.
    • This is the latest in a series of serious Secure Email Gateway and AsyncOS flaws involving malicious email attachments or parsing, including actively exploited CVE-2026-76461 and CVE-2025-20393.
    Key Points
    • 01Cisco patched CVE-2026-76519, an actively exploited flaw in Secure Email Gateway that can let a remote unauthenticated attacker execute commands with root privileges.
    • 02The flaw is caused by improper handling of email attachments in the Advanced Malware Protection feature and can be triggered by sending a maliciously crafted attachment through an unpatched device.
    • 03Affected systems have the File Reputation service enabled and assigned to a mail policy and run Content Scanner Tools earlier than version 25.3.0.5525.
    • 04Cisco advised administrators to check Content Scanner Tools versions, review compromise indicators, upgrade to a fixed release, and examine firewall and network logs for suspicious external data transfers.
    • 05Cisco said it deployed mitigations on cloud instances and contacted Cisco Secure Email Cloud device owners where it found evidence of a potential compromise.

In plain words

Cisco says criminals are actively using a serious weakness in its Secure Email Gateway, a product organizations use to screen email for spam and harmful files. The problem affects physical and virtual gateways that have File Reputation enabled and an older scanning-tools update; a specially made email attachment could allow an outsider to take full control of the system. This matters because a compromised email gateway may expose an organization’s communications and provide a foothold for further harm, so affected customers should install Cisco’s available update and check for signs of compromise.

Summary
Cisco warns that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76519, a critical Cisco Secure Email Gateway flaw that can let unauthenticated senders write files and execute commands as root. Organizations should immediately update Content Scanner Tools to 25.3.0.5525 or later or upgrade to a fixed AsyncOS release, then check appliances for compromise.

Cisco warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76519, a critical vulnerability in Cisco Secure Email Gateway. A sender without a login can send an email with a crafted attachment that writes files to the appliance’s operating system and could lead to commands being run as root. Cisco found the flaw through internal security scanning and became aware of attacks in October, but did not disclose the number of affected devices, the responsible actors, or whether attackers obtained root access. Cisco has contacted managed Secure Email Cloud customers whose devices showed possible compromise indicators.

The issue affects physical and virtual gateways only when the File Reputation service is enabled in a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools is older than version 25.3.0.5525. Cisco says the fastest remediation is updating Content Scanner Tools to version 25.3.0.5525 or later, while fixed AsyncOS releases include 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780; there is no fixed 16.0 build. Administrators can run grep "System Security" system_logs to look for compromise indicators, although Cisco warns that a clean result is not proof because a root-level attacker could conceal evidence. For compromised virtual appliances, Cisco advises preserving forensic data before rebuilding a new fixed instance, recreating its configuration without importing the old one, and renewing credentials and cryptographic material.

  • The scanner-tools update can be installed without an AsyncOS software upgrade or appliance restart, making it the fastest remediation path for eligible supported releases.
  • A clean appliance scan is not definitive because an attacker with full administrative control could remove or conceal evidence; Cisco advises reviewing firewall and network logs outside the appliance for unusual external data transfers.
  • For a compromised virtual appliance, upgrading it can destroy forensic logs and evidence, so Cisco recommends preserving data first and rebuilding a new instance rather than importing the prior configuration.
  • One compromised cluster member may expose the SSH keys used among members, so Cisco recommends restoring every appliance in any cluster containing a compromised gateway.
  • Cisco had already shipped fixes in its September hardening release, but assigned this flaw its own CVE and advisory after learning it was being actively exploited.
Key Points
  • 01Cisco says attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76519, a critical Cisco Secure Email Gateway flaw that can allow an unauthenticated sender to write files to the appliance operating system and potentially run commands as root.
  • 02The issue affects physical and virtual gateways only when File Reputation is enabled and Content Scanner Tools is older than version 25.3.0.5525.
  • 03Cisco says the flaw is fixed by Content Scanner Tools version 25.3.0.5525 or later, or by AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780.
  • 04Administrators can check for attempted exploitation by running grep "System Security" system_logs on each appliance in a cluster.
  • 05Cisco recommends rebuilding compromised virtual appliances on a fixed release without importing the old configuration and renewing appliance credentials and cryptographic material.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an actively exploited critical (CVSS 9.8) flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that can allow unauthenticated attackers to potentially execute commands as root. Affected organizations need to urgently verify scanner versions, apply the available fix, and investigate systems for compromise.

In plain words

Microsoft released fixes for 1,413 security problems in Windows, Office, SharePoint, SQL Server, and other software, including one Windows problem that criminals are already using. That flaw can let a harmful file sent through email or a message get around Windows warnings if a person is persuaded to open or click it. Businesses, government agencies, and anyone using affected Microsoft software should install the updates, because some problems could let attackers run unauthorized programs, view sensitive information, or disrupt systems.

Summary
Microsoft released patches for a record 1,413 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell flaw actively exploited to bypass Mark of the Web protections. Organizations should prioritize the exploited Windows Shell bug and publicly disclosed .NET WDAC bypass, then use Microsoft's risk cohorts to triage the broader update set.

Microsoft released patches for a record 1,413 vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, Developer Tools, SharePoint Server, SQL Server, and other products. More than 670 of the flaws involve privilege escalation, over 300 involve remote code execution, and more than 70 are rated Critical. The release includes an actively exploited Windows Shell command injection vulnerability, CVE-2026-96951, which has a CVSS score of 8.8.

Microsoft said CVE-2026-96951 can allow an attacker to evade Mark of the Web protections through a specially crafted file, although the attacker must convince a user to click a link or interact with a malicious attachment. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and directed U.S. federal agencies to apply fixes by October 16, 2026. Other notable fixes include the publicly known CVE-2026-108398 .NET Framework flaw, which can bypass Windows Defender Application Control, and CVE-2026-21413 in Raw Image Extension, which can be triggered when Windows previews a crafted RAW image file. Microsoft also introduced risk cohorts to help organizations group related CVEs for prioritization while assessing exploitation status, severity, attack path, user interaction, and product-specific guidance.

  • The update volume is exceptionally high, but the article emphasizes that organizations should prioritize flaws with active exploitation, public disclosure, and relevant attack conditions rather than treating every CVE equally.
  • The actively exploited Windows Shell issue requires an attacker to persuade a user to interact with a crafted file or link, showing that email and instant-message delivery remain relevant despite the technical flaw being in Windows.
  • The .NET Framework issue is especially significant after an attacker already has local access because it can bypass Windows Defender Application Control without requiring user interaction.
  • The Raw Image Extension flaw can be triggered when Windows creates a thumbnail or preview of a crafted RAW image, meaning the user does not need to open the image file for the issue to occur.
  • Microsoft's new risk cohorts are intended to group CVEs that need similar customer assessment, while still requiring organizations to review each flaw's exploitation status, severity, attack path, user interaction requirements, and affected product guidance.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft released patches for 1,413 vulnerabilities, including 1,102 in Windows, 134 in Office, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server.
  • 02CVE-2026-96951 is a Windows Shell command injection flaw with a CVSS score of 8.8 that Microsoft said has been actively exploited to evade Mark of the Web protections.
  • 03CISA added CVE-2026-96951 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and required U.S. federal agencies to apply fixes by October 16, 2026.
  • 04Microsoft said the publicly known CVE-2026-108398 flaw in .NET Framework could allow an authenticated local attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control and execute code in a protected process.
  • 05Microsoft also patched CVE-2026-21413, a CVSS 9.8 heap-based buffer overflow in Raw Image Extension that can enable remote code execution when Windows generates a thumbnail or preview of a crafted RAW image file.

The update also addresses publicly known WDAC-bypass and high-severity RAW image preview flaws across widely used Microsoft products, making prompt prioritization highly relevant.

In plain words

Palo Alto Networks released updates for a serious flaw in software used to manage certain network-protection devices, and says attackers have already used it in a small number of cases. Someone who already has valid login details and can reach the device’s management page could take full control of it. Organizations using affected Palo Alto firewalls should install the updates quickly and limit management access to trusted internal addresses, because a compromised device could put their wider network at risk.

Summary
Palo Alto Networks patched CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity PAN-OS management-interface flaw that allows authenticated attackers with network access to execute code as root and has already seen limited exploitation. Organizations should urgently update affected firewalls and restrict management-interface access to trusted internal IP addresses.

Palo Alto Networks released security updates for CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity PAN-OS flaw affecting the management interface of certain firewalls and management appliances. The company said it has observed very limited exploitation targeting that interface. The vulnerability has a severity score of 8.6 and can allow authenticated attackers with network access to execute code as root on vulnerable devices.

Affected systems include PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, as well as Panorama virtual and M-Series appliances; Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit after Internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView refrigeration controllers were switched into defrost mode, with most exposed devices running outdated firmware vulnerable to known flaws. Attackers switched hundreds of French supermarket refrigerators into defrost mode on the night of 11 October, causing spoiled food and, in some cases, fires. The incident involved Internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView refrigeration-controller management interfaces. Censys found that, before the attack, France accounted for 61% of identified exposed StoreView control panels, and most ran versions where an administrator password could be derived from the current date.

Danfoss had previously patched CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451, and CVE-2025-41452, while Claroty researchers demonstrated in August 2026 that the first two flaws could be chained to achieve remote code execution. In France, exposed StoreView hosts fell from 1,825 on 11 October to 537 on 14 October, with patched and unpatched devices declining at roughly the same rate, indicating operators were taking controllers off the Internet rather than patching them. CERT-FR issued an emergency alert calling for immediate removal of the controllers from the Internet, and the article notes that outdated firmware remains widespread globally despite version 5.3.2 being current.

  • The current StoreView release was version 5.3.2, but the largest exposed groups on the day of the incident were versions 3.3.0, 4.3.1, and 3.2.6.

In plain words

Researchers investigated attackers who broke into a telecommunications provider’s central Fortinet management system and stole settings, passwords, security keys, and network details for more than 500 customer and company firewalls. The attackers then used this access to watch some network traffic, log in remotely, and install a hidden program that runs only in the device’s memory, making it difficult to find. This matters because one compromised management system can expose many separate organizations at once, and replacing software alone may not be enough if stolen passwords and digital keys are not also changed.

Summary
Unit 42 found that attackers exploited a FortiManager flaw to steal configurations, credentials, and trust material for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls, then used that access for traffic sniffing, VPN access, and management impersonation. They also deployed PEERSTITCH, a memory-resident FortiOS implant that patches core processes and evades conventional disk- and network-based detection.

Unit 42 investigated a September 2024 intrusion at a telecommunications managed service provider, tracked as CL-STA-0954 (also known as UNC5820). Attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575 on the provider’s FortiManager appliance, then exfiltrated an archive containing configurations, encrypted credentials, cryptographic trust material, and information for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. The affected firewalls protected both the provider’s infrastructure and client networks, although the investigation did not confirm compromise of those client networks. The article emphasizes that centralized management platforms can expose a large downstream environment when compromised.

The attackers used stolen information to establish FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions, push packet-capture rules to intercept selected traffic, and potentially impersonate FortiManager to obtain additional firewall configurations. They also exploited CVE-2025-61624 to deploy PEERSTITCH, an ARM64 implant that patches the memory of the FortiOS miglogd and iked processes rather than persisting as a file or opening a network port. PEERSTITCH uses existing process traffic and cross-process memory writes to communicate and alter VPN-session handling, while the attackers also used Apache mod_md and ACME challenge handling to establish a reverse-shell channel. Unit 42 advises that after a management-platform compromise, organizations should treat the credentials and certificates it held as compromised and rotate them in addition to patching the affected system.

  • A compromise of one FortiManager appliance exposed not only the provider’s own environment but also configuration, credential, and trust material for more than 500 downstream firewalls in client networks, illustrating the unusually broad impact of centralized management-system access.
  • PEERSTITCH avoids conventional detection by operating only in memory, using legitimate FortiOS processes’ existing traffic rather than opening ports or making its own outbound connections.
  • The implant creates a covert communication path by writing data directly between the memory of FortiOS logging and VPN processes through /proc/<pid>/mem, then uses matching session tags to alter VPN processing behavior.
  • Attackers used FortiOS auto-script path traversal to write files outside the expected script directory as root, including a loader for PEERSTITCH and a malicious Apache configuration used to trigger reverse-shell commands.
  • Useful hunting evidence can remain even when the implant removes its files: defenders can examine miglogd and iked for anonymous 16 KB executable-and-writable memory regions, unexpected cross-process memory writes, altered code locations, crash logs, and auto-script names containing ../../.
Key Points
  • 01Unit 42 investigated a September 2024 intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider tracked as CL-STA-0954, also known as UNC5820.
  • 02The attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575 on a FortiManager appliance and exfiltrated an archive containing configurations, credential material, cryptographic keys, and information on more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls.
  • 03The attackers pushed unauthorized packet-capture configurations to managed FortiGate devices to collect unencrypted HTTP traffic and traffic associated with targeted services, including TFTP, RADIUS, and LDAP.
  • 04By exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers deployed PEERSTITCH, an ARM64 implant that patches the memory of FortiOS logging and VPN processes without leaving a persistent binary or opening a listening port.
  • 05The article advises organizations to treat credentials and certificates held by a compromised edge-management platform as compromised and rotate them, even after the platform is patched.

Microsoft, Health-ISAC, and several partners disrupted three services that criminals used to create fake messages and websites pretending to be trusted companies. Since January 2026, these services allegedly helped send more than one billion scam emails and text messages to over 75,000 organizations in more than 150 countries, including Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. The scams targeted consumers, hospitals, banks, and businesses to steal login and financial details, which can then be used for fraudulent purchases and money transfers. The action matters because it also struck a marketplace that supplied criminals with the accounts, online storage, and tools needed to run scams at large scale.

Summary
Microsoft, Health-ISAC, and partners disrupted the Chinese-language phishing ecosystem behind CoGUI, Haozi, and Iron Man System, which allegedly enabled more than one billion scam messages targeting 75,000 organizations worldwide. The operation also targeted YAM Store, a marketplace supplying compromised cloud accounts, infrastructure, and phishing kits to cybercriminals.

Microsoft, Health-ISAC, the Japan Cybercrime Control Center, and private-sector partners disrupted the CoGUI, Haozi, and Iron Man System phishing kits through a court-authorized operation. Microsoft said the operators behind the kits facilitated more than one billion phishing emails and text messages sent to more than 75,000 organizations worldwide since January 2026. The investigation began in late 2025 after malicious messaging campaigns targeted people in Japan. The messages affected consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries.

Microsoft tracks YAM Store as Storm-3119 and the developers of the three kits as Storm-2990. YAM Store advertised the phishing kits alongside access to compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft and Google cloud environments, and it allegedly resold hijacked accounts, licenses, and online storage. The group reportedly took over viable cloud environments, granted itself broad Microsoft Graph and SharePoint permissions, and used SharePoint and OneDrive for bulk hosting. CoGUI, Haozi, and Iron Man System offered templates impersonating government, financial, logistics, and consumer brands to steal sign-in credentials and financial information.

Iron Man System had thousands of phishing templates tailored to brands in more than 130 countries and used measures such as fake CAPTCHA pages, IP-based access controls, and Telegram alerts. The kits captured information entered by victims through WebSocket connections, allowing operators to monitor victims’ progress in real time. Resecurity said Iron Man required regular contact with a vendor licensing server, creating a dependency that defenders could disrupt by disabling or redirecting that authorization host. Microsoft said the disruption makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools, and infrastructure used to operate large-scale scams.

  • The phishing ecosystem operated as a supply chain: YAM Store provided compromised or fraudulent cloud environments and resold hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage, while Storm-2990 supplied phishing kits to customers.
  • Iron Man System’s requirement to regularly contact a vendor licensing server created a centralized dependency; Resecurity noted that disabling or sinkholing that authorization host could impair every active deployment.
  • The kits used real-time WebSocket capture of victims’ submitted information, allowing operators to watch responses as they happened and determine the next page shown to a target.
  • Storm-3119 allegedly turned compromised Microsoft 365 tenants’ SharePoint and OneDrive storage into bulk-hosting capacity that could be sold to other criminals.
  • The operation began after campaigns targeting people in Japan were reported, but the associated services were linked to messages affecting organizations in more than 150 countries.

In plain words

A flaw in Linux, the software that runs many computers and servers, can let someone with access to a machine take full control of it. In some virtual-machine setups, it can also let a person controlling a virtual computer interfere with the real computer hosting it. The issue affects Linux versions used by several major providers and organizations, so installing the available fix is important to prevent unauthorized control or service disruption.

Summary
CVE-2026-74580 (Vghost) is a Linux vhost flaw that can let local users gain root privileges and, in certain virtualized configurations, allow a guest VM to write into the host QEMU process. Organizations should install kernels containing the cache-invalidation fix and restrict access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock until patched.

Tencent Zhuque Lab disclosed CVE-2026-74580, dubbed Vghost, a flaw in Linux’s vhost subsystem that can allow a local user to read and write kernel memory and gain root access. The issue affects kernels from Linux 4.11 through 7.2-rc4, and Tencent demonstrated local-user-to-root exploitation on Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. The article says there is no public indication that the flaw has been exploited.

The bug stems from vhost retaining old memory-mapping cache entries when live virtual-ring addresses or sizes are changed. With a device IOTLB attached, later checks can be skipped, causing the kernel to use stale address translations and read from or write outside the intended mapped region. In certain virtual-machine setups using a virtual IOMMU, iommu_platform, and device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can write into the host’s QEMU process and potentially take control of it or crash it.

An upstream fix clears the cache whenever a ring is reconfigured, and the article recommends installing a fixed kernel and rebooting. Until then, administrators can reduce the local-user risk by restricting access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock and limiting the owning group to trusted virtualization services. The article states that there is no interim workaround for the guest-to-host escape path, making a patched kernel the only remedy for that scenario.

  • The local privilege-escalation path is described as deterministic, requiring neither memory grooming nor lucky timing.
  • Exposure varies substantially by system configuration: Ubuntu limited the relevant device node to the kvm group, while four tested distributions exposed it as world-readable, allowing any local user to reach it.
  • The flaw resulted from the interaction of two otherwise reasonable changes made years apart: a 2017 cache shortcut and a 2020 change that delayed address checks.
  • Restricting access to vhost device nodes can reduce the local-user risk before patching, but the article states there is no temporary workaround for the guest-to-host escape path.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-74580, also called Vghost, is a Linux vhost subsystem flaw that can allow a local user to read and write kernel memory and gain root access.
  • 02In specific virtual-machine configurations using a virtual IOMMU and device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can use the flaw to write outside intended bounds into the host's QEMU process.
  • 03The flaw affects Linux kernels from version 4.11 through 7.2-rc4, and Tencent reproduced local-user-to-root exploitation on Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux, Microsoft Azure Linux, and Oracle Linux.
  • 04The upstream fix clears vhost memory-mapping cache data whenever a virtual ring is reconfigured, and the article recommends installing a patched kernel and rebooting.
  • 05Until systems are patched, the article recommends restricting access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock; it states that only a patched kernel remedies the guest-to-host path.

This is a high-impact Linux kernel vulnerability that can enable deterministic local root access and, in specific virtualized configurations, guest-to-host compromise. It affects a long range of kernel versions and several major distribution families, making patching and vhost device access controls broadly relevant, although no public exploitation has been reported.

Researchers say a Chinese-speaking group used an AI-powered testing tool called ARTEX to break into customer and employee web services run by several South Korean financial companies. This matters because the stolen data could be used for scams or fraud, and AI tools can make it easier for attackers to search for weak points and break into organizations at scale.

Summary
A Chinese-speaking, financially motivated threat actor allegedly used the ARTEX agentic AI pentesting framework to automate reconnaissance and exploit SQL injection and authentication-bypass flaws in South Korean financial web applications, stealing PII for about 67,000 people. The incident shows that LLM-enabled offensive tooling can lower the barrier to large-scale intrusion and data theft.

Zscaler ThreatLabz analyzed a campaign that abused ARTEX, an open-source AI-driven penetration-testing framework, to target multiple South Korean financial institutions. First observed in late September 2026, the campaign reportedly resulted in the theft of personally identifiable information for approximately 67,000 people. ThreatLabz assessed with moderate confidence that the activity was conducted by a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking threat actor. The attackers targeted internet-facing customer inquiry portals and employee mobile-application backends rather than core banking infrastructure.

ARTEX coordinates language models and worker agents to perform reconnaissance, identify weaknesses, execute tools, and retain findings for subsequent actions. In this campaign, it used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary model, with Zhipu AI GLM-5.3 and xAI Grok 4.6 for supplementary reasoning, and the agents exploited SQL injection and authentication-bypass flaws. The stolen records included names, phone numbers, annual income figures, and loan limits, while Claude Code sessions were used to seek advice about selling the data and locating Korean-language Telegram channels. The article notes that ARTEX’s default safeguards blocked government and university targets but did not restrict financial institutions, and recommends controls such as stronger authorization checks, rate limits, monitoring for enumeration, and isolating open-source testing harnesses from production systems.

  • ARTEX’s built-in targeting restrictions blocked government and university domains by default but did not cover financial institutions, leaving the affected sector outside its default scope controls.
  • The campaign focused on peripheral, internet-facing applications rather than core banking infrastructure, showing that customer portals and employee mobile-service backends can expose sensitive financial records.
  • ARTEX’s workflow lets a planning model select subsequent actions based on results returned by tool-executing worker agents, enabling reconnaissance and exploitation to be coordinated across multiple LLM services.
  • The article recommends enforcing testing boundaries through software configuration and code rather than relying only on instructions given to an AI model.
  • After the abuse was publicly disclosed, ARTEX’s developer made the project closed source, but the article notes that previously downloaded copies and forks may still be available.

In plain words

Researchers at XBOW used an OpenAI model to help find and combine three previously unknown flaws in Google Chrome, allowing a malicious web page to take control of a Windows computer without the person clicking or downloading anything. Google fixed the flaws and paid XBOW $250,000; Chrome users should restart their browser and ensure it is updated to version 152.0.7977.82 or later. The work shows that AI can greatly reduce the time and cost needed to create serious attacks, potentially putting the many people who use Chrome on Windows at greater risk if they do not keep software updated.

Summary
XBOW researchers used OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol agents to develop a full Chrome-to-Windows exploit chain in six days for roughly $40,000, earning Google's $250,000 maximum reward. Google has patched the three flaws in Chrome 152; users should restart and update to version 152.0.7977.82 or later.

XBOW researchers said they built a full Google Chrome exploit chain in six days using AI agents running OpenAI’s publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. The chain combined three previously unknown Chrome flaws and could run code on a Windows computer when a user simply loaded a web page, without requiring a click or download. Google confirmed and fixed the flaws, then awarded XBOW its maximum \(250,000 full-chain reward. XBOW estimated the AI work cost about \)40,000.

The attack crossed Chrome’s two nested protective barriers, moving from a web page to code execution outside the browser on Windows. A V8 JavaScript-engine flaw gave memory control, an animated-WebP decoder flaw enabled a precise memory write beyond the inner barrier, and a Crashpad flaw turned that write into full code execution. The identified flaws, CVE-2026-85045 and CVE-2026-78952, were fixed in Chrome 152.0.7977.82 and 152.0.7977.65, respectively. Users should restart Chrome and verify that they are running version 152.0.7977.82 or later, because automatic updates do not take effect until the browser is relaunched.

XBOW said the six-day sprint followed months of prior work, including an earlier full Chrome chain that took two months to produce. The company said its AI agents searched Chrome source code, tested ideas, created proofs of concept, and drafted exploit code, while human researchers selected targets, provided context, checked results, and combined the pieces. XBOW also said the exploit’s modular design let it replace a component after finding that Google already knew about one flaw used in an earlier version. The company presented the result as evidence that serious Chrome exploit chains can now be produced more quickly and at lower cost.

  • The six-day result followed months of preparation and XBOW’s earlier two-month effort to produce its first full Chrome exploit chain, so the headline sprint was not a standing start.
  • XBOW designed the exploit as replaceable components, which allowed researchers to substitute one part after learning that Google already knew about a flaw the original chain used.
  • Although Chrome updates automatically, the protections from these fixes do not take effect until users restart the browser.
  • The AI agents performed source-code searches, testing, proof-of-concept work, and initial exploit drafts, while researchers selected targets, supplied context, checked results, and chose which components to combine.

  • 02The chain combined three previously unknown Chrome flaws to let a person who merely loads a malicious web page run code outside Chrome on a Windows computer without clicking or downloading anything.

In plain words

Attackers used a flaw in an optional Nextcloud document-editing add-on from Collabora to place hidden files on some servers that could let them run commands remotely. The risk affects people and small teams using the Built-in CODE Server add-on, especially during a restart, update, or crash; separate Collabora servers and installations using only the regular Nextcloud Office app are not affected. This matters because the attackers searched compromised servers for passwords and cryptocurrency-wallet files, so any data the server could access may have been exposed.

Summary
Attackers actively exploited CVE-2026-110447 in Collabora Online’s Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud to execute unauthenticated commands and install PHP web shells when the local document server was down. Administrators should upgrade richdocumentscode to 26.4.303 or later or remove it entirely, as merely disabling the app does not mitigate the flaw.

Attackers exploited CVE-2026-110447 in Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, an optional Nextcloud app also called richdocumentscode, to run commands without authentication and install PHP web shells on Nextcloud servers. The first reported attacks occurred on September 10, and three administrators reported compromises involving version 26.4.302. The vulnerability affects Built-in CODE Server versions before 26.4.303, while standalone Collabora Online servers and installations using only the regular Nextcloud Office app are not affected.

The vulnerable proxy.php script started the local CODE server when no service was listening, but it inserted request content into a shell command that allowed embedded commands to run. As a result, exploitation was possible when the local document server was down, including during restarts, upgrades, or crashes. Reported attackers placed files named like shx*.php, searched for credential stores and cryptocurrency-wallet files, and attempted failed sudo commands, although the reports did not show root access or confirmed file exfiltration.

Collabora released version 26.4.303 on September 11 and later published an advisory stating that affected users must update or remove the app, because disabling it alone does not fix the issue. Nextcloud 29 and older cannot install the fixed release, so users of those versions need to upgrade Nextcloud or remove Built-in CODE Server. Administrators are advised to check for shx*.php files, review logs for suspicious proxy.php?status requests, and treat data readable by the web server account as potentially exposed.

  • Disabling the Built-in CODE Server app does not remove the risk because its proxy.php file can still be run directly by the web server; the app must be updated or removed.
  • The attack is limited to periods when the local CODE service is unavailable, making restarts, upgrades, and crashes particularly important times to review logs for suspicious requests.
  • Users running Nextcloud 29 or older cannot install the fixed Built-in CODE Server release and may still receive an affected version from the app store, so removal or a Nextcloud upgrade is necessary.
  • The reported intrusions did not show file uploads or data theft, but the attackers searched for password databases and cryptocurrency-wallet files, meaning all data readable by the web server account should be considered potentially exposed.
  • The initial correction was committed before the first reported attack but was released without identifying the issue as a security fix, while the public advisory and CVE were published later.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers exploited CVE-2026-110447 in Collabora Online’s Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud to run commands without logging in and place PHP web shells on affected servers.
  • 02The flaw affects richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and can be triggered only when the app’s local document server is not running, such as during a restart, upgrade, or crash.
  • 03Collabora said users must update richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later or remove it, because disabling the app alone does not address the issue.
  • 04Nextcloud 29 and older cannot install the fixed version, so users of those versions should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the Built-in CODE Server app.
  • 05Administrators who reported intrusions found web shells in the app’s folder and observed attacker searches for credential stores and cryptocurrency-wallet files.

Helpers in the United States kept company laptops at their homes and made the overseas workers appear to be working from inside the country, allowing about $3 million in pay to be sent abroad. The scheme allegedly generated about $3 million for North Korea and continues to evolve through identity theft, device spoofing, subcontractors, and coercion.

The U.S. Department of Justice charged 14 people and seized about 187 computers in connection with a North Korean remote IT worker scheme that affected more than 70 U.S. companies. Two U.S. citizens were arrested, while the remaining charged defendants were at large. Authorities also dismantled more than 40 laptop farms in Texas that were used to make overseas workers appear to be based in the United States.

According to court documents, the scheme operated from around 2019 through July 2025 and generated approximately $3 million for the workers, with funds allegedly supporting North Korea’s government, nuclear weapons, and military programs. U.S.-based facilitators allegedly hosted company-issued laptops, opened bank and money-transfer accounts, and helped workers use fraudulent identities to obtain remote jobs. The FBI and CrowdStrike said the operation has evolved through redirected laptop shipments, false stolen-device reports, spoofed device identifiers, subcontracted work and interviews, and, in some cases, threats against former managers and their families.

  • Laptop farms provide more than a place to store devices: they create a rented U.S. address, identity, and financial footprint that helps the operators satisfy bank verification requirements.
  • The scheme can conceal the true worker even after hiring because North Korean workers reportedly subcontract assigned work to freelancers in Pakistan, India, Nigeria, and nearby countries for a fraction of the salary.
  • Operators reportedly manipulated laptop delivery and replacement processes by filing false theft reports, claiming sudden relocations, and using staffing firms to redirect employer-issued devices without the staffing firms’ knowledge.
  • The FBI identified an escalation in which operators allegedly threatened former managers and their families with physical violence to demand payments or force actions supporting the scheme.
  • CrowdStrike assessed that shutting down the identified laptop farms will likely have only localized, temporary effects because the operators are expected to adapt their methods.

In plain words

A flaw in curl, a widely used tool and software component for moving data online, could let a malicious website take over the computer that uploads a sufficiently large file to it. It affects curl and libcurl versions 8.12.0 through 8.22.0 when they use HTTP/2, including programs that rely on libcurl behind the scenes. The attack is difficult and will more often crash a program, but it can be turned into code execution under the right conditions, so users should update to version 8.23.0 or use HTTP/1.1 until they can update.

Summary
curl and libcurl 8.12.0–8.22.0 contain CVE-2026-92392, an HTTP/2 upload use-after-free that a malicious, trusted server can potentially turn into client-side code execution. Upgrade to curl 8.23.0 or a listed backported release, or temporarily force HTTP/1.1.

curl fixed CVE-2026-92392 in version 8.23.0, addressing an HTTP/2 upload flaw that can corrupt memory on the uploading client. The use-after-free affects curl and libcurl versions 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, including applications that use libcurl for data transfers. A public proof of concept showed that a malicious server could turn the issue into code execution on the client machine.

The attack requires a client to upload a roughly 135KB file over HTTP/2 to an attacker-controlled server whose certificate passes the client’s checks. The server can stall and reset the upload stream so that curl retains and later uses a pointer to a freed transfer object; the proof of concept then uses leaked memory addresses and overwritten data to redirect execution. curl said successful code execution requires detailed knowledge of the target’s build, memory layout, allocator, timing, and a very small payload, making a crash the more likely outcome. Users should upgrade to curl 8.23.0 or an available backported release, or temporarily force HTTP/1.1 if updating is not yet possible.

  • The attacker does not need to compromise the client directly; the vulnerable behavior can be triggered by a server receiving an upload, provided its certificate passes the client’s checks.
  • Temporarily forcing HTTP/1.1 can avoid the affected upload path, although curl notes that an application may reuse an existing connection using a different protocol version.
  • The code fix was a six-line reorder that delays releasing HTTP/2 references to a transfer handle until remaining upload data has been flushed.
  • The reported code-execution demonstration required exact target build and memory-layout knowledge, coordinated timing across two transfers, and a payload of roughly 23 bytes, so curl said a crash is the more likely result of an attempted real-world attack.
Key Points
  • 01curl fixed CVE-2026-92392, an HTTP/2 upload use-after-free flaw, in curl 8.23.0 on October 14.
  • 02The issue affects curl and libcurl versions 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, including applications that use libcurl for transfers.
  • 03A malicious server can trigger the flaw when a client uploads a roughly 135KB file over HTTP/2 and accepts the server's certificate.
  • 04The public proof of concept demonstrated code execution on the uploading machine, although curl said a real exploit requires precise knowledge of the target's build and memory layout and would more likely cause a crash.
  • 05Users should upgrade to curl 8.23.0 or a listed backported release, or temporarily force HTTP/1.1 if they cannot update.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a high-severity patch for curl and libcurl, widely used transfer software and libraries, with a public proof of concept demonstrating client-side code execution. Although no exploitation has been reported and reliable exploitation is difficult, affected users should upgrade or disable HTTP/2 uploads.

It can trick people into installing a harmful second app and even replacing a real banking app with a lookalike version that disables some of the bank app’s safety checks. People using targeted banking and wallet apps—especially in Indonesia, but also across several other countries—could have their passwords, payment PINs, text messages, screen activity, and phone control stolen. The campaign has replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while its credential targeting spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand. Hirudo can steal credentials, payment PINs, SMS messages, screen and camera content, and provide operators with remote control of infected devices.

    Hirudo’s standout capability is replacing a genuine banking app with a purpose-built tampered copy that can bypass security checks from inside the app. The malware detects a target banking app, checks its signing certificate, opens Android’s uninstaller for the genuine app, and downloads a bank-specific replacement in parallel.     • Blocking internet access with a broken VPN does not fully defeat Google Play Protect because it can still detect known harmful apps offline, but it may reduce cloud-based reputation and code-analysis checks.

In plain words

Researchers found a new Android threat called Hirudo that tricks people into installing seemingly normal shopping, adult-content, or short-drama apps, then offers a fake update. It can remove a person’s real banking app and replace it with a lookalike version designed to hide warning signs and steal bank passwords, payment PINs, text messages, screen images, and audio. It has been seen posing as Indonesian banks and also targets financial organizations in China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand, putting victims’ money and personal information at risk.

Summary
Hirudo is an Android banking trojan that uses fake app updates and Accessibility permissions to replace legitimate banking apps with patched copies that bypass signature, Accessibility, screenshot, and Play Integrity checks. It has targeted banks primarily in Indonesia and can steal credentials, PINs, SMS messages, screenshots, and audio while enabling real-time remote control.

ThreatFabric reported on Hirudo, an Android banking malware that replaces legitimate banking apps with modified copies to bypass security checks and steal account credentials. It has been observed impersonating at least seven Indonesian banks and also targets financial organizations in China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand. Hirudo is delivered through seemingly legitimate shopping, adult-content, and short-drama apps that show a fake update notification and request permissions, including Accessibility access.

After installation, Hirudo launches the real banking app’s uninstaller, downloads a patched copy, and uses Accessibility permission to install it. The altered app retains most original code but uses a hooking engine based on YAHFA and Dobby to substitute signing-certificate information, hide Accessibility services, remove screenshot protections, and modify attestation and Play Integrity requests. Hirudo can steal banking passwords, payment PINs, device-unlock secrets, and SMS messages, stream screens, record audio, and access both cameras.

ThreatFabric found thousands of application-credential entries plus device, lock-screen, and financial-profile data in an unsecured backend panel, though the total victim count is unknown. The researchers said the malware shifts attacks toward security mechanisms inside hardened banking applications, while noting that leaked attestation key material and revoked certificates can allow server-side detection. They recommend that banks perform integrity and attestation validation on the server, tie checks to sessions and protected actions, and keep behavioral and transaction-risk controls.

  • Hirudo does not merely imitate banking screens; it modifies and runs within the banking app itself, allowing it to interfere with the app’s own security checks.
  • The app-replacement process is risky for the malware because a victim can interrupt it while the legitimate app is being removed or while the modified replacement is being installed.
  • Hirudo’s certificate-forgery approach has a known weakness: its bundled key material was publicly leaked, and Google has identified two associated certificates as compromised, enabling server-side checks to detect them.
  • ThreatFabric found thousands of application-credential entries and device, lock-screen, and financial-profile data in an unsecured Hirudo backend panel, although the total number of victims is unknown.
  • The article recommends that banks validate app integrity on their servers and tie those checks to individual sessions and sensitive actions, rather than relying only on checks performed on the phone.
Key Points
  • 01Hirudo is an Android banking malware family that replaces legitimate banking apps with modified copies intended to bypass security checks and steal account credentials.
  • 02It is distributed through seemingly functional shopping, adult-content, and short-drama apps that display a fake update prompt and request permissions, including Accessibility access.
  • 03After installation, Hirudo can uninstall the legitimate banking app, download a patched version, and use Accessibility permissions to install it.
  • 04The patched apps can substitute signing-certificate information, hide enabled Accessibility services, remove screenshot protection, and alter key-attestation and Play Integrity requests.
  • 05ThreatFabric observed Hirudo impersonating at least seven Indonesian banks and reported that it also targets financial organizations in China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand.

Polish investigators say the company behind Pegasus, NSO Group, could technically access information collected when Poland’s former government used the phone-spying software against opposition leaders, independent prosecutors, and hundreds of other people. The information was sent through servers outside Poland, and the officials running the program reportedly lacked full control over how it worked. Although investigators cannot confirm that NSO viewed any particular person’s data, the case raises concerns that governments using foreign-made spying tools may expose their citizens’ private information to outside organizations or countries.

Summary
Polish investigators say NSO Group retained technical access to the Pegasus system used by Poland’s former government, creating the possibility that surveillance data on opposition figures and other victims was exposed outside the country. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the operation a major state scandal, though prosecutors have not established that NSO actually accessed specific intercepted materials.

Polish investigators said an analysis by the Internal Security Agency found that the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau did not have full control over the Pegasus spyware system it used under Poland’s former government. The National Prosecutor’s Office said the server component used to infect mobile devices remained under NSO Group’s exclusive control, and the bureau lacked passwords for many accounts with administrator-level access. Prosecutors said this prevented full verification of system components involved in transmitting and storing collected information.

The investigation found that collected data was routed outside Poland through an anonymizing network using foreign servers and IP addresses, while NSO supplied remote updates and technical support without interrupting surveillance operations. Prosecutors said NSO therefore had technical access to information from operational inspections, but they could not determine whether the company actually accessed material from any particular inspection. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the former government’s use of Pegasus one of Poland’s largest scandals since the fall of communism, saying opposition leaders, independent prosecutors, his wife and daughter, and more than 500 other people were among those targeted or infected.

  • The agency operating Pegasus reportedly lacked passwords for many administrator-level accounts, meaning it could not fully verify how system components handled the transmission and storage of collected data.

In plain words

Ledger has told sellers in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to stop selling its cryptocurrency wallets after some devices were secretly altered before customers bought them. The altered wallets could capture the 24-word backup phrase that gives someone control of a person’s crypto funds, then send it to an unauthorized party. Confirmed losses involve devices sold by CryptoBilis, while reports also involve other sellers in Asia and Europe, showing why physical products can be risky if they are changed somewhere in the sales chain.

Summary
Ledger has halted reseller sales across Southeast Asia and Hong Kong after discovering tampered wallets sold by CryptoBilis contained LTE-enabled implants that stole 24-word recovery phrases. The company says its direct sales channel is safe while it investigates reports involving other Asian and European retailers.

Ledger has told distributors and resellers in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it investigates hardware implant incidents. The move followed confirmation that some devices sold by CryptoBilis had been altered and used to steal customers’ cryptocurrency recovery phrases. Ledger said confirmed fund losses involve CryptoBilis devices, although users have also reported suspected compromised devices purchased from sellers in Asia and Europe.

Ledger’s Donjon security team said the implant is a separate component that detects and decodes the 24-word recovery phrase used to set up or restore a wallet. It then sends the phrase over LTE through a provisioned eSIM, while leaving the Secure Element, Ledger operating system, transactions, and signatures unchanged. Because of this, Ledger’s integrity self-checks do not detect the implant; the company said its infrastructure, services, and direct sales channel remain safe to use.

Reports linked suspected modified devices to a Metapod retailer in Singapore and MediaMarkt in Europe, and MediaMarkt has removed Ledger products from shelves. Trezor said it has found no evidence that its devices were compromised, but it plans to reduce its reseller network and revoke affected sellers’ authorization on January 1, 2027. Trezor said the change is intended to improve oversight of how devices are sourced, stored, and handled.

  • Ledger's built-in integrity checks did not detect the implant because it was a separate component and did not modify the Secure Element, Ledger operating system, transactions, or signatures.
  • The implant was designed to capture the recovery phrase during wallet setup or restoration and send it over LTE, meaning it could expose access to funds without changing the wallet's visible transaction behavior.
  • Although confirmed losses were tied to CryptoBilis, reports involving retailers in Singapore and Europe prompted a sales halt across a much broader regional distributor network.
  • Trezor's decision to end affected reseller partnerships despite finding no evidence of compromised devices shows that reseller sourcing, storage, and handling are being treated as supply-chain security concerns.

Its targets included agencies involved in diplomacy, economic development, environmental management, water resources, and energy, using convincing documents and files that secretly install remote-control software. Researchers believe the group may be connected to Kazakhstan and is seeking information that could affect regional negotiations, resource planning, and energy security, especially amid the effects of the Russia–Ukraine war.

Summary
Cisco Talos and Recorded Future linked UAT-6275 (also tracked as TAG-193/Silent Lynx) to sustained espionage campaigns against government and resource-sector targets across Central Asia and the CIS, with medium-confidence evidence of a Kazakhstan nexus. The group uses malicious documents, PowerShell/GitHub payloads, custom reverse shells, and a WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploit to gain persistent access.

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group investigated UAT-6275, tracked by Recorded Future as TAG-193, which targeted government organizations across Central Asia and the wider Commonwealth of Independent States. Targets and lure themes spanned Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus. The article notes that the group’s interest in diplomacy, resource management, and energy infrastructure may relate to the intelligence value of regional developments and the effects of the Russia–Ukraine war. It recommends monitoring for unexpected PowerShell activity, downloads from public services such as GitHub, new scheduled tasks, and Windows Startup-folder changes. Four-Byte Write and Timing Bug Let Researchers Run Code in Windows SmartScreen Enclave

82
In plain words

Researchers found a flaw in a protected part of Windows that helps Microsoft’s anti-phishing feature compare passwords without exposing them. A program already running on a Windows 11 computer with deep access could use the flaw to run its own code in that protected area, though the researchers did not show passwords being stolen and no real-world abuse has been reported. Microsoft fixed the issue in its September 8, 2026 update, and the finding matters because these protected areas are designed to remain safe even if other parts of a computer have been taken over.

Summary
Researchers showed that flaws in Windows SmartScreen’s SFAPE VBS enclave could let a local attacker with an existing foothold execute code inside the protected VTL1 environment. Microsoft patched CVE-2026-83498 in its September 8, 2026 Windows 11 update; installing KB5124008 is the recommended mitigation.

Security researchers at Doyensec demonstrated code execution inside SFAPE.dll, a protected Windows VBS enclave used by Microsoft Defender SmartScreen’s Enhanced Phishing Protection. The enclave stores a hashed form of a Windows sign-in password so Windows can detect when the password is entered into unsafe locations. The research was a lab proof of concept, has not been seen in real attacks, and did not demonstrate theft of a user’s password.

The attack requires code already running locally with low-level access that can load and call the enclave, such as LSASS on Windows 11 systems. Doyensec combined a repeated initialization call that makes a fixed four-byte write to a caller-controlled address with a timing bug, eventually replacing the table that determines which code the enclave may run. Microsoft fixed CVE-2026-83498 in the September 8, 2026 cumulative update KB5124008 for Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, including a policy that blocks the old vulnerable SFAPE enclave from loading. Doyensec noted that Windows lacks a general blocklist for vulnerable enclaves and that an older Microsoft Edge enclave affected by CVE-2023-36880 remains loadable.

Summary
Microsoft released the October 2026 cumulative updates KB5127648 and KB5127646 to fix Always On VPN connections that could become stuck or fail after September Windows 11 updates. Microsoft released the KB5127648 and KB5127646 cumulative updates to fix Always On VPN connection failures caused by the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates. The issue affected fully updated Windows 11 24H2 and later systems using automatic protocol selection or fallback between IKEv2 and SSTP. Always On VPN automatically creates a secure connection to an organization’s network when a device connects to the internet.

When the initial VPN connection attempt failed, affected connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state, fail to reconnect, or show an error stating that the specified port was already in use. Organizations unable to install the October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates immediately can work around the issue by configuring their Always On VPN profiles to use only SSTP or only IKEv2. Microsoft said organizations should choose the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements.

  • The Always On VPN problem was not necessarily visible on the first attempt: it specifically occurred when the initial connection failed and the system then tried to select or fall back to another connection method.
  • Organizations that cannot deploy the October update immediately have a documented workaround: disable automatic protocol selection and configure either SSTP-only or IKEv2-only connections.
  • The update-related disruption extended beyond remote access, as Microsoft also had to issue emergency fixes for Remote Desktop Services, Hyper-V, and USB audio issues linked to the September 2026 updates.
  • The recommended temporary protocol choice is not universal; Microsoft says organizations should select SSTP or IKEv2 according to their own environment, security, and deployment requirements.

A senior finance leader at a UK medical-device and infection-prevention manufacturer received a Teams-styled email claiming a company document was ready. Its VIEW & COMPLETE button opened a genuine Microsoft authorization endpoint, while the readable URL embedded in the request pointed to a nonexistent subdomain of the victim’s own company. The message was designed to make the link appear like a plausible internal sign-in or verification path.

The request used an unknown third-party OAuth client ID, prompt=none, and permissions for identity information and Microsoft Graph User.Read. Its uri value was not a documented Microsoft authorization parameter, and the link omitted the documented required redirect_uri and response_type parameters, meaning the visible hostname did not establish the real reply destination. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, composite authentication, and URL reputation checks all passed, but IRONSCALES identified VIP impersonation at 85 confidence and quarantined the affected mailbox; the article states there was no evidence anyone clicked.

  • A readable URL inside an OAuth sign-in link can be deliberate decoration: the article found that the only visible destination was carried in an undocumented uri parameter and did not determine where the authorization flow would send a response.
  • When redirect_uri is absent from an OAuth link, the actual reply location may exist only in the third-party app’s registration, so examining the OAuth client ID is more actionable than judging the visible hostname.
  • The phishing message passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, composite authentication, and URL-reputation checks because it used legitimate Microsoft-hosted links and an established sending domain, showing why those checks alone did not identify it.
  • The use of prompt=none was designed to let the Microsoft authorization request proceed without displaying user interface, making an unsolicited OAuth link especially concerning.
  • The article states that an automated analysis treated the fake company subdomain as a plausible sign-in destination, demonstrating that the planted value was capable of misleading link analysis as well as recipients.

Package managers have an integrity problem
